{{Short description|All points for which two tangents of a curve intersect at 90° angles}}
{{For|the branch of medicine|Orthoptics}}

In the [[geometry]] of [[curve]]s, an '''orthoptic''' is the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of points for which two [[tangent]]s of a given curve meet at a right angle.

[[File:Parabel-orthop.svg|right|thumb|
{{legend-line|solid red|[[Parabola]]}}
{{legend-line|solid purple|Orthoptic of the parabola (its [[Generatrix|directrix]])}}
]]
[[File:Orthoptic-ellipse-s.svg|thumb|{{legend-line|solid red|[[Ellipse]]}}
{{legend-line|solid purple|Orthoptic of the ellipse (its [[director circle]])}}
{{legend-line|solid green|[[Minimum bounding box]] of the ellipse ([[circumscribed]] by the orthoptic circle)}}
{{legend-line|dashed black|[[Semi-major and semi-minor axes|Major and minor axes]] of the ellipse}}]]
[[File:Orthoptic-hyperbola-s.svg|thumb|{{legend-line|solid red|[[Hyperbola]]}}
{{legend-line|solid purple|Orthoptic of the hyperbola (its director circle)}}
{{legend-line|dashed black|{{mvar|xy}}-axes and hyperbolic [[asymptote]]s}}]]

Examples:
# The orthoptic of a [[parabola]] is its directrix (proof: see [[#Orthoptic of a parabola|below]]),
# The orthoptic of an [[ellipse]] <math>\tfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \tfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1</math> is the [[director circle]] <math>x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2</math> (see [[#Ellipse|below]]),
# The orthoptic of a [[hyperbola]] <math>\tfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \tfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1,\ a > b</math> is the director circle <math>x^2 + y^2 = a^2 - b^2</math> (in case of {{math|''a'' ≤ ''b''}} there are no orthogonal tangents, see [[#Hyperbola|below]]),
# The orthoptic of an [[astroid]] <math>x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = 1</math> is a [[quadrifolium]] with the polar equation <math>r=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(2\varphi), \ 0\le \varphi < 2\pi</math> (see [[#Orthoptic of an astroid|below]]). 

Generalizations:
# An '''isoptic''' is the set of points for which two tangents of a given curve meet at a ''fixed angle''  (see [[#Isoptic of a parabola, an ellipse and a hyperbola|below]]).
# An '''isoptic''' of ''two'' plane curves is the set of points for which two tangents meet at a ''fixed angle''.
# [[Thales' theorem]] on a [[Chord (geometry)|chord]] {{mvar|PQ}} can be considered as the orthoptic of two circles which are degenerated to the two points {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|Q}}.

==Orthoptic of a parabola ==
Any parabola can be transformed  by a [[rigid motion]] (angles are not changed) into a parabola with equation <math>y = ax^2</math>. The slope at a point of the parabola is <math>m = 2ax</math>. Replacing {{mvar|x}} gives the parametric representation of the parabola with the tangent slope as parameter: <math> \left(\tfrac{m}{2a},\tfrac{m^2}{4a} \right) \! .</math> The tangent has the equation <math>y=mx+n</math> with the still unknown {{mvar|n}}, which can be determined by inserting the coordinates of the parabola point. One gets <math> y=mx-\tfrac{m^2}{4a}\; .</math>

If a tangent contains the point {{math|(''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>)}}, off the parabola, then the equation
<math display="block">y_0 = m x_0 -\frac{m^2}{4a} \quad \rightarrow \quad m^2 - 4ax_0\,m + 4ay_0 = 0</math>
holds, which has two solutions {{math|''m''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''m''<sub>2</sub>}} corresponding to the two tangents passing {{math|(''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>)}}. The free term of a reduced quadratic equation is always the product of its solutions. Hence, if the tangents meet at {{math|(''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>)}} orthogonally, the following equations hold: 
<math display="block">m_1 m_2 = -1 = 4 a y_0</math>
The last equation is equivalent to
<math display="block">y_0 = -\frac{1}{4a}\, , </math>
which is the equation of the [[Parabola#Parabola as graph of a function|directrix]].

== Orthoptic of an ellipse and hyperbola ==
=== Ellipse ===
{{main|Director circle}}
Let <math> E:\; \tfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \tfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 </math> be the ellipse of consideration. 

# The tangents to the ellipse <math>E</math> at the vertices and co-vertices intersect at the 4 points <math>(\pm a, \pm b)</math>, which lie on the desired orthoptic curve (the circle <math> x^2+y^2 = a^2 + b^2</math>).
# The tangent at a point <math>(u,v)</math> of the ellipse <math>E</math> has the equation <math>\tfrac{u}{a^2} x + \tfrac{v}{b^2} y = 1</math> (see [[Ellipse#Tangent|tangent to an ellipse]]). If the point is not a vertex this equation can be solved for {{mvar|y}}: <math> y = -\tfrac{b^2u}{a^2v}\;x\; + \;\tfrac{b^2}{v}\, .</math>

Using the abbreviations
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\begin{align}
 m &= -\tfrac{b^2u}{a^2v},\\
 \color{red}n &= \color{red}\tfrac{b^2}{v}
\end{align} </math>|{{EquationRef|I}}}}
and the equation <math> {\color{blue}\tfrac{u^2}{a^2} = 1 - \tfrac{v^2}{b^2} = 1-\tfrac{b^2}{n^2}} </math> one gets:
<math display="block">m^2 = \frac{b^4 u^2}{a^4 v^2} = \frac{1}{a^2} {\color{red}\frac{b^4}{v^2}} {\color{blue}\frac{u^2}{a^2}} = \frac{1}{a^2} {\color{red}n^2} {\color{blue}\left(1-\frac{b^2}{n^2}\right)} = \frac{n^2-b^2}{a^2}\, .</math>
Hence 
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> n = \pm\sqrt{m^2 a^2 + b^2}</math>|{{EquationRef|II}}}}
and the equation of a non vertical tangent is
<math display="block">y = m x \pm \sqrt{m^2 a^2 + b^2}.</math>
Solving relations {{EquationNote|I|(I)}} for <math>u,v</math> and respecting {{EquationNote|II|(II)}} leads to the slope depending parametric representation of the ellipse: 
<math display="block">(u,v) = \left(-\tfrac{ma^2}{\pm\sqrt{m^2a^2+b^2}}\;,\;\tfrac{b^2}{\pm\sqrt{m^2a^2+b^2}}\right)\, . </math> (For another proof: see {{slink|Ellipse#Parametric representation}}.)

If a tangent contains the point <math>(x_0,y_0)</math>, off the ellipse, then the equation
<math display="block">y_0 = m x_0 \pm \sqrt{m^2a^2+b^2}</math>
holds. Eliminating the square root leads to
<math display="block">m^2 - \frac{2x_0y_0}{x_0^2-a^2}m + \frac{y_0^2-b^2}{x_0^2-a^2} = 0,</math>
which has two solutions <math>m_1,m_2</math> corresponding to the two tangents passing through <math>(x_0,y_0)</math>. The constant term of a monic quadratic equation is always the product of its solutions. Hence, if the tangents meet at <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> orthogonally, the following equations hold: 
[[File:Orthoptic locus of a circle, ellipses and hyperbolas.gif|thumb|right|Orthoptics (red circles) of a circle, ellipses and hyperbolas]]
<math display="block">m_1 m_2 = -1 = \frac{y_0^2 - b^2}{x_0^2 - a^2}</math>
The last equation is equivalent to
<math display="block">x_0^2+y_0^2 = a^2+b^2\, .</math>
From '''(1)''' and '''(2)''' one gets:
{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = The intersection points of orthogonal tangents are points of the circle <math>x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2</math>.}}

=== Hyperbola ===
The ellipse case can be adopted nearly exactly to the hyperbola case. The only changes to be made are to replace <math>b^2</math> with <math>-b^2</math> and to restrict {{mvar|m}} to {{math|{{abs|''m''}} > {{sfrac|''b''|''a''}}}}. Therefore:
{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = The intersection points of orthogonal tangents are points of the circle <math>x^2 + y^2 = a^2 - b^2</math>, where {{math|''a'' > ''b''}}.}}

== Orthoptic of an astroid ==
[[File:Orthoptic-astroid.svg|thumb|Orthoptic (purple) of an astroid]]
An astroid can be described by the parametric representation
<math display="block">\mathbf c(t) = \left(\cos^3t, \sin^3t\right), \quad 0 \le t < 2\pi.</math>
From the condition
<math display="block">\mathbf \dot c(t) \cdot \mathbf \dot c(t+\alpha) = 0</math>
one recognizes the distance {{mvar|α}} in [[parameter space]] at which an orthogonal tangent to {{math|'''ċ'''(''t'')}} appears. It turns out that the distance is independent of parameter {{mvar|t}}, namely {{math|1=''α'' = ± {{sfrac|π|2}}}}. The equations of the (orthogonal) tangents at the points {{math|'''c'''(''t'')}} and {{math|'''c'''(''t'' + {{sfrac|π|2}})}} are respectively:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
y &= -\tan t \left(x-\cos^3 t\right) + \sin^3 t, \\
y &= \frac{1}{\tan t} \left(x+\sin^3 t\right) + \cos^3 t.
\end{align}</math>
Their common point has coordinates:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= \sin t \cos t \left(\sin t - \cos t\right), \\
y &= \sin t \cos t \left(\sin t + \cos t\right).
\end{align}</math>
This is simultaneously a parametric representation of the orthoptic.

Elimination of the parameter {{mvar|t}} yields the implicit representation 
<math display="block">2\left(x^2+y^2\right)^3 - \left(x^2-y^2\right)^2 = 0.</math>
Introducing the new parameter {{math|1=''φ'' = ''t'' − {{sfrac|5π|4}}}} one gets
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos(2\varphi)\cos\varphi, \\
y &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos(2\varphi)\sin\varphi.
\end{align}</math>
(The proof uses the [[angle sum and difference identities]].) Hence we get the polar representation
<math display="block">r = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos(2\varphi), \quad 0 \le \varphi < 2\pi</math> 
of the orthoptic. Hence:
{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = The orthoptic of an astroid is a [[quadrifolium]].}}

== Isoptic of a parabola, an ellipse and a hyperbola ==
[[File:Isoptic-80-parabola-s.svg|thumb|Isoptics (purple) of a parabola for angles 80° and 100°]]
[[File:Isoptic-ellipse-s.svg|thumb|Isoptics (purple) of an ellipse for angles 80° and 100°]]
[[File:Isoptic-hyperbola-s.svg|thumb|Isoptics (purple) of a hyperbola for angles 80° and 100°]]
Below the isotopics for angles {{math|''α'' ≠ 90°}} are listed. They are called {{mvar|α}}-isoptics. For the proofs see [[#proofs|below]].

=== Equations of the isoptics ===
; Parabola<nowiki>:</nowiki>
The {{mvar|α}}-isoptics of the parabola with equation {{math|1=''y'' = ''ax''<sup>2</sup>}} are the branches of the hyperbola
<math display="block">x^2-\tan^2\alpha\left(y+\frac{1}{4a}\right)^2-\frac{y}{a}=0.</math>
The branches of the hyperbola provide the isoptics for the two angles {{mvar|α}} and {{mvar|180° − ''α''}} (see&nbsp;picture).

; Ellipse<nowiki>:</nowiki>
The {{mvar|α}}-isoptics of the ellipse with equation {{math|1={{sfrac|''x''<sup>2</sup>|''a''<sup>2</sup>}} + {{sfrac|''y''<sup>2</sup>|''b''<sup>2</sup>}} = 1}} are the two parts of the degree-4 curve
<math display="block">\left(x^2+y^2-a^2-b^2\right)^2 \tan^2\alpha = 4\left(a^2y^2 + b^2x^2 - a^2b^2\right)</math>
(see&nbsp;picture).

; Hyperbola<nowiki>:</nowiki>
The {{mvar|α}}-isoptics of the hyperbola with the equation {{math|1={{sfrac|''x''<sup>2</sup>|''a''<sup>2</sup>}} − {{sfrac|''y''<sup>2</sup>|''b''<sup>2</sup>}} = 1}} are the two parts of the degree-4 curve
<math display="block">\left(x^2 + y^2 - a^2 + b^2\right)^2 \tan^2\alpha = 4 \left(a^2y^2 - b^2x^2 + a^2b^2\right).</math>

=== Proofs ===
; Parabola<nowiki>:</nowiki>
A parabola {{math|1=''y'' = ''ax''<sup>2</sup>}} can be parametrized by the slope of its tangents {{math|1=''m'' = 2''ax''}}:
<math display="block">\mathbf c(m) = \left(\frac{m}{2a},\frac{m^2}{4a}\right), \quad m \in \R.</math>

The tangent with slope {{mvar|m}} has the equation 
<math display="block">y=mx-\frac{m^2}{4a}.</math>

The point {{math|(''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>)}} is on the tangent if and only if
<math display="block">y_0 = m x_0 - \frac{m^2}{4a}.</math> 

This means the slopes {{math|''m''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|''m''<sub>2</sub>}} of the two tangents containing {{math|(''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''y''<sub>0</sub>)}} fulfil the quadratic equation 
<math display="block">m^2 - 4ax_0m + 4ay_0 = 0.</math>

If the tangents meet at angle {{mvar|α}} or {{math|180° − ''α''}}, the equation 
<math display="block">\tan^2\alpha = \left(\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1 m_2}\right)^2</math>

must be fulfilled. Solving the quadratic equation for {{mvar|m}}, and inserting {{math|''m''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|''m''<sub>2</sub>}} into the last equation, one gets
<math display="block">x_0^2-\tan^2\alpha\left(y_0+\frac{1}{4a}\right)^2-\frac{y_0}{a} = 0.</math>

This is the equation of the hyperbola above. Its branches bear the two isoptics of the parabola for the two angles {{mvar|α}} and {{math|180° − ''α''}}.

; Ellipse<nowiki>:</nowiki>
In the case of an ellipse {{math|1={{sfrac|''x''<sup>2</sup>|''a''<sup>2</sup>}} + {{sfrac|''y''<sup>2</sup>|''b''<sup>2</sup>}} = 1}} one can adopt the idea for the orthoptic for the quadratic equation
<math display="block">m^2-\frac{2x_0y_0}{x_0^2-a^2}m + \frac{y_0^2-b^2}{x_0^2-a^2} = 0.</math>

Now, as in the case of a parabola, the quadratic equation has to be solved and the two solutions {{math|''m''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|''m''<sub>2</sub>}} must be inserted into the equation
<math display="block">\tan^2\alpha=\left(\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right)^2.</math>

Rearranging shows that the isoptics are parts of the degree-4 curve:
<math display="block">\left(x_0^2+y_0^2-a^2-b^2\right)^2 \tan^2\alpha = 4\left(a^2y_0^2+b^2x_0^2-a^2b^2\right).</math>

; Hyperbola<nowiki>:</nowiki>
The solution for the case of a hyperbola can be adopted from the ellipse case by replacing {{math|''b''<sup>2</sup>}} with {{math|−''b''<sup>2</sup>}} (as in the case of the orthoptics, see&nbsp;[[#Orthoptic of an ellipse and a hyperbola|above]]).

To visualize the isoptics, see [[implicit curve]].
